claim: CB1-iLTD in acute rat hippocampal slices was associated with protein synthesis-dependent presynaptic structural changes.
source: We found that CB1-iLTD in acute rat hippocampal slices was associated with protein synthesis-dependent presynaptic structural changes.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding directly in the abstract, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in increased ribosomal proteins and initiation factors.
source: Using proteomics, we determined that CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in increased ribosomal proteins and initiation factors, but decreased levels of proteins involved in regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such as ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1, and presynaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in decreased levels of proteins involved in regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such as ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1.
source: Using proteomics, we determined that CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in increased ribosomal proteins and initiation factors, but decreased levels of proteins involved in regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such as ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1, and presynaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in decreased levels of presynaptic release proteins.
source: Using proteomics, we determined that CB1 activation in hippocampal neurons resulted in increased ribosomal proteins and initiation factors, but decreased levels of proteins involved in regulation of the actin cytoskeleton, such as ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1, and presynaptic release.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC proteomics data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CB1-iLTD increased ubiquitin/proteasome activity.
source: Moreover, while CB1-iLTD increased ubiquitin/proteasome activity, ubiquitination but not proteasomal degradation was critical for structural and functional presynaptic CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ubiquitination but not proteasomal degradation was critical for structural and functional presynaptic CB1-iLTD.
source: Moreover, while CB1-iLTD increased ubiquitin/proteasome activity, ubiquitination but not proteasomal degradation was critical for structural and functional presynaptic CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5B, 5C, and 5D.

claim: CB1-iLTD relies on both protein synthesis and ubiquitination to elicit structural changes that underlie long-term reduction of GABA release.
source: Thus, CB1-iLTD relies on both protein synthesis and ubiquitination to elicit structural changes that underlie long-term reduction of GABA release.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript, including Figures 1, 3, and 5.

claim: Presynaptic forms of plasticity are widely expressed in the brain but their mechanism remains poorly understood.
source: While presynaptic forms of plasticity, that is long-term synaptic strengthening (long-term potentiation or LTP) and weakening (long-term depression or LTD) due to long-lasting increase and decrease in neurotransmitter release, respectively, are widely expressed in the brain, their mechanism remains poorly understood (Castillo, 2012; Monday and Castillo, 2017; Monday et al., 2018; Yang and Calakos, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Type-1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1)-mediated LTD is a ubiquitous form of long-lasting reduction of transmitter release.
source: A good example of a ubiquitous form of long-lasting reduction of transmitter release is type-1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1)-mediated LTD (Araque et al., 2017; Castillo et al., 2012; Heifets and Castillo, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Endogenous cannabinoids (eCBs) are released upon activity and travel in a retrograde manner to bind presynaptic CB1.
source: Here, endogenous cannabinoids (eCBs) are released upon activity and travel in a retrograde manner to bind presynaptic CB1, a Gi/o-coupled receptor, resulting in CB1-LTD at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about eCB signaling.

claim: CB1 is a Gi/o-coupled receptor.
source: Here, endogenous cannabinoids (eCBs) are released upon activity and travel in a retrograde manner to bind presynaptic CB1, a Gi/o-coupled receptor, resulting in CB1-LTD at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CB1 receptor signaling.

claim: CB1 activation results in CB1-LTD at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: Here, endogenous cannabinoids (eCBs) are released upon activity and travel in a retrograde manner to bind presynaptic CB1, a Gi/o-coupled receptor, resulting in CB1-LTD at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Induction of long-term eCB-mediated plasticity requires extended (minutes) CB1 activation.
source: Induction of long-term eCB-mediated plasticity requires extended (minutes) CB1 activation (Chevaleyre and Castillo, 2003; Chevaleyre et al., 2007; Ronesi, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Presynaptic protein synthesis is required for CB1-LTD.
source: Although the presynaptic changes downstream CB1 that suppress transmitter release in a long-term manner remain unclear, there is evidence that presynaptic protein synthesis is required (Yin et al., 2006; Younts et al., 2016), but what proteins are synthesized and the precise role of these proteins in CB1-LTD is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: What proteins are synthesized and the precise role of these proteins in CB1-LTD is unclear.
source: Although the presynaptic changes downstream CB1 that suppress transmitter release in a long-term manner remain unclear, there is evidence that presynaptic protein synthesis is required (Yin et al., 2006; Younts et al., 2016), but what proteins are synthesized and the precise role of these proteins in CB1-LTD is unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Proteostatic mechanisms are vital for neuronal function and synaptic plasticity.
source: Proteostatic mechanisms, the cellular processes that balance protein synthesis and degradation, are vital for neuronal function and synaptic plasticity (Biever et al., 2019; Birdsall and Waites, 2019; Cohen and Ziv, 2019; Liang and Sigrist, 2018; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In postsynaptic forms of plasticity, local protein synthesis has been tightly correlated with both consolidation of LTP and structural changes.
source: In postsynaptic forms of plasticity, such as NMDA receptor-dependent LTP, local protein synthesis has been tightly correlated with both consolidation of LTP and structural changes (Bosch et al., 2014; Ostroff et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2008; Tominaga-Yoshino et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synthesis of β-actin, AMPA receptors, and CaMKII proteins may be critical for the increase in dendritic spine volume and synapse strength associated with LTP.
source: In particular, synthesis of β-actin, AMPA receptors, and CaMKII proteins may be critical for the increase in dendritic spine volume and synapse strength associated with LTP (Bramham, 2008; Nakahata and Yasuda, 2018; Rangaraju et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Concurrent regulation of protein degradation through the proteasome and lysosome is required for activity-dependent pre- and postsynaptic changes in synapse strength.
source: Concurrent regulation of protein degradation through the proteasome and lysosome is also required for activity-dependent pre- and postsynaptic changes in synapse strength (Biever et al., 2019; Cohen and Ziv, 2017; Hegde, 2017; Monday et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is evidence for rapid (<30 min) presynaptic protein synthesis under basal conditions and during plasticity.
source: We and others have recently provided evidence for rapid (<30 min) presynaptic protein synthesis under basal conditions and during plasticity (Hafner et al., 2019; Younts et al., 2016), but whether these newly synthesized proteins participate in CB1-LTD by regulating presynaptic structural changes is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Whether newly synthesized proteins participate in CB1-LTD by regulating presynaptic structural changes is unknown.
source: We and others have recently provided evidence for rapid (<30 min) presynaptic protein synthesis under basal conditions and during plasticity (Hafner et al., 2019; Younts et al., 2016), but whether these newly synthesized proteins participate in CB1-LTD by regulating presynaptic structural changes is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Presynaptic structure and function are controlled by actin polymerization and depolymerization.
source: Presynaptic structure and function are controlled by actin polymerization and depolymerization (Cingolani and Goda, 2008; Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Branched actin filaments in the presynaptic compartment provide a scaffold for synaptic vesicles and the active zone.
source: Branched actin filaments in the presynaptic compartment provide a scaffold for synaptic vesicles and the active zone (Michel et al., 2015; Rust and Maritzen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Structural changes of the presynaptic terminal are associated with altered synapse strength.
source: Moreover, structural changes of the presynaptic terminal are associated with altered synapse strength (Gundelfinger and Fejtova, 2012; Matz et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2014; Monday and Castillo, 2017), and the size of the presynaptic terminal and active zone has been correlated with the postsynaptic response (Bartol et al., 2015; Bourne et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The size of the presynaptic terminal and active zone has been correlated with the postsynaptic response.
source: Moreover, structural changes of the presynaptic terminal are associated with altered synapse strength (Gundelfinger and Fejtova, 2012; Matz et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2014; Monday and Castillo, 2017), and the size of the presynaptic terminal and active zone has been correlated with the postsynaptic response (Bartol et al., 2015; Bourne et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CB1 receptor activation can trigger ultrastructural changes in vesicle distribution associated with short-term CB1-mediated plasticity.
source: There is evidence that CB1 activation alters the ultrastructural vesicle distribution in CB1-expressing (CB1+) boutons on short time scales (García-Morales et al., 2015; Ramírez-Franco et al., 2014) and leads to retraction of growth cones in developing axons (Roland et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CB1 activation leads to retraction of growth cones in developing axons.
source: There is evidence that CB1 activation alters the ultrastructural vesicle distribution in CB1-expressing (CB1+) boutons on short time scales (García-Morales et al., 2015; Ramírez-Franco et al., 2014) and leads to retraction of growth cones in developing axons (Roland et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is not known whether CB1-LTD is associated with morphological changes in presynaptic structure in the mature mammalian brain.
source: However, it is not known whether CB1-LTD is associated with morphological changes in presynaptic structure in the mature mammalian brain.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: WIN 55,212–2 (5 µM) bath application for 25 min induces CB1-iLTD.
source: To induce CB1-iLTD the CB1 agonist WIN 55,212–2 (5 µM) was bath applied for 25 min, and induction was confirmed by monitoring extracellular field inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (fIPSPs), which allows non-invasive, stable long-term assessment of inhibitory synaptic transmission (Heifets et al., 2008; Younts et al., 2016; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CB1-iLTD is associated with a significant decrease of CB1 bouton volume.
source: Using CB1 immunolabeling, which accurately approximates bouton volume (Dudok et al., 2015), we found that CB1-iLTD is associated with a significant decrease of CB1 bouton volume (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The structural change in CB1 bouton volume was long-lasting as it persisted for 60 min after WIN treatment.
source: This structural change was long-lasting as it persisted for 60 min after WIN treatment (Figure 1C), and it was blocked by concurrent bath application with protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX, 80 µM), demonstrating a requirement for protein synthesis (Figure 1C,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The WIN-induced decrease in CB1 bouton volume was blocked by concurrent bath application with protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX, 80 µM).
source: This structural change was long-lasting as it persisted for 60 min after WIN treatment (Figure 1C), and it was blocked by concurrent bath application with protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX, 80 µM), demonstrating a requirement for protein synthesis (Figure 1C,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CHX alone did not affect basal bouton volume.
source: CHX alone did not affect basal bouton volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WIN treatment increased the proportion of small CB1 boutons.
source: This overall shrinkage by WIN treatment was driven by an increase in the proportion of the small CB1 boutons and a trend toward a decrease in large boutons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Volume of parvalbumin (PV+) boutons in the CA1 pyramidal layer was not altered by WIN application.
source: This effect was specific because volume of parvalbumin (PV+) boutons in the CA1 pyramidal layer was not altered by WIN application (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), as assessed by immunolabeling for PV boutons (Younts et al., 2016), which do not express CB1 receptors (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: PV boutons do not express CB1 receptors.
source: This effect was specific because volume of parvalbumin (PV+) boutons in the CA1 pyramidal layer was not altered by WIN application (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B), as assessed by immunolabeling for PV boutons (Younts et al., 2016), which do not express CB1 receptors (Glickfeld and Scanziani, 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bassoon size within CB1+ boutons was significantly decreased following WIN application.
source: As a complementary approach, we used Bassoon immunolabeling to assess the size of the presynaptic active zone. Similar to the total bouton volume, Bassoon size within CB1+ boutons was also significantly decreased following WIN application and this effect was blocked by CHX treatment (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: The WIN-induced decrease in Bassoon size within CB1+ boutons was blocked by CHX treatment.
source: As a complementary approach, we used Bassoon immunolabeling to assess the size of the presynaptic active zone. Similar to the total bouton volume, Bassoon size within CB1+ boutons was also significantly decreased following WIN application and this effect was blocked by CHX treatment (Figure 1D–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: The volume of vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) was markedly reduced in CB1+ boutons by WIN treatment.
source: We also found that the volume of vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT), a well-established marker of inhibitory synapses, was markedly reduced in CB1+ boutons by WIN treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: CB1-iLTD is associated with a protein-synthesis-dependent shrinkage of CB1+ boutons, which may contribute to the long-lasting reduction in neurotransmitter release observed in this form of plasticity.
source: These results strongly suggest that CB1-iLTD is associated with a protein-synthesis-dependent shrinkage of CB1+ boutons, which may contribute to the long-lasting reduction in neurotransmitter release observed in this form of plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Protein synthesis is required for both structural and functional presynaptic changes involved in CB1-iLTD.
source: Along with our previous study (Younts et al., 2016), our findings indicate that protein synthesis is required for both structural and functional presynaptic changes involved in CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in the current study and a previous study.

claim: CB1-dependent increases in protein synthesis were evident after brief CB1 activation in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: We previously showed CB1-dependent increases in protein synthesis were evident after brief CB1 activation in cultured hippocampal neurons (Younts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Two populations of cultured rat hippocampal neurons were labeled using distinct combinations of 'medium' or 'heavy' stable-isotope weight variants of Arginine and Lysine for SILAC analysis.
source: Two populations of cultured rat hippocampal neurons ('medium' and 'heavy') were labeled using distinct combinations of 'medium' or 'heavy' stable-isotope weight variants of Arginine and Lysine.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A high degree of correlation was observed between forward and reverse SILAC experiments.
source: To strengthen the robustness of findings, we performed a replicate 'reverse' experiment where 'heavy' neurons were treated with WIN and observed a high degree of correlation between replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Components of the protein synthesis machinery were upregulated following CB1 activation.
source: Consistent with previous studies of axonal mRNAs, components of the protein synthesis machinery were upregulated (Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016), as well as the protein degradation machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data and citations to previous literature.

claim: Components of the protein degradation machinery were upregulated following CB1 activation.
source: Consistent with previous studies of axonal mRNAs, components of the protein synthesis machinery were upregulated (Hafner et al., 2019; Shigeoka et al., 2016), as well as the protein degradation machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data.

claim: A number of presynaptic proteins were downregulated following CB1 activation.
source: A number of presynaptic proteins were downregulated following CB1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1 were significantly downregulated following CB1 activation.
source: Notably, two key regulators of the actin cytoskeleton, Actin-related protein 2/3 complex subunit 2 (ARPC2) and Wiscott-Aldrich Associated Protein family (WASF1/WAVE1) were significantly downregulated, suggesting these proteins could be implicated in the reduction of neurotransmitter release and presynaptic volume associated with CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1 could be implicated in the reduction of neurotransmitter release and presynaptic volume associated with CB1-iLTD.
source: Notably, two key regulators of the actin cytoskeleton, Actin-related protein 2/3 complex subunit 2 (ARPC2) and Wiscott-Aldrich Associated Protein family (WASF1/WAVE1) were significantly downregulated, suggesting these proteins could be implicated in the reduction of neurotransmitter release and presynaptic volume associated with CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the SILAC data.

claim: The top cluster of enriched GO terms represented upregulated terms related to 'Protein synthesis and processing'.
source: In accordance with translational upregulation following CB1 activation (Younts et al., 2016), the top cluster represented upregulated GO terms related to 'Protein synthesis and processing' (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The second cluster of enriched GO terms was composed of terms relating to 'Neuronal projections'.
source: The second cluster was composed of GO terms relating to 'Neuronal projections', suggestive of the structural change associated with CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The third cluster of enriched GO terms was associated with 'Energy metabolism'.
source: The third cluster was GO terms associated with 'Energy metabolism' which may be representative of the previously reported CB1-mediated decrease in cellular respiration (Hebert-Chatelain et al., 2016; Mendizabal-Zubiaga et al., 2016; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous literature.

claim: 43 proteins were upregulated by CB1 activation.
source: Among the differentially expressed proteins, we found that 43 proteins were upregulated and 56 proteins were downregulated by CB1 activation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 56 proteins were downregulated by CB1 activation.
source: Among the differentially expressed proteins, we found that 43 proteins were upregulated and 56 proteins were downregulated by CB1 activation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both protein synthesis and coincident degradation of structural and presynaptic proteins occur downstream of CB1 activation.
source: Together, these results suggest that both protein synthesis and coincident degradation of structural and presynaptic proteins occur downstream of CB1 activation, and could therefore be implicated in CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the SILAC data.

claim: CB1 directly interacts with Rac1 and members of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC).
source: CB1 directly interacts with Rac1 and members of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC), which includes actin branching modulators WASF1/WAVE1 and Arp2/3 (Njoo et al., 2015), and these proteins are downregulated in hippocampal neurons following CB1 activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and SILAC data.

claim: WASF1/WAVE1 and Arp2/3 are actin branching modulators.
source: CB1 directly interacts with Rac1 and members of the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC), which includes actin branching modulators WASF1/WAVE1 and Arp2/3 (Njoo et al., 2015), and these proteins are downregulated in hippocampal neurons following CB1 activation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Regulation of the abundance of ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1 may represent a mechanism underlying structural and functional presynaptic changes involved in CB1-iLTD.
source: Therefore, regulation of the abundance of these proteins may represent a mechanism underlying structural and functional presynaptic changes involved in CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the data.

claim: JSK application blocked the WIN-induced decrease in presynaptic bouton volume.
source: Using the same high-resolution microscopy and 3D reconstruction as Figure 1, we activated CB1 in the presence of jasplakinolide (JSK, 250 nM), a reagent that promotes actin polymerization (Holzinger, 2009). We found that JSK application blocked the WIN-induced decrease in presynaptic bouton volume (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Actin dynamics likely underlie the structural changes following CB1 activation.
source: These results indicate that actin dynamics likely underlie the structural changes following CB1 activation.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the JSK experiment.

claim: Bath application of JSK impaired CB1-iLTD.
source: Similar to the effects on structural plasticity, bath application of JSK impaired CB1-iLTD (Figure 3B), whereas JSK application alone had no effect on basal synaptic transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: JSK application alone had no effect on basal synaptic transmission.
source: Similar to the effects on structural plasticity, bath application of JSK impaired CB1-iLTD (Figure 3B), whereas JSK application alone had no effect on basal synaptic transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Actin remodeling is critical for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
source: These results strongly suggest that actin remodeling is critical for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the JSK experiments.

claim: CB1-iLTD was impaired by application of NSC (30 µM, 25 min) during induction.
source: To test the role of this pathway, we inhibited Rac1 activity using NSC 23766 (NSC), an inhibitor of Rac1-GEF interaction (Gao et al., 2004). CB1-iLTD was impaired by application of NSC (30 µM, 25 min) during induction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NSC alone transiently suppressed inhibitory transmission.
source: NSC alone transiently suppressed inhibitory transmission (Figure 3D), unlike excitatory transmission (Hou et al., 2014), and this effect was associated with a decrease in PPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting Rac1 activity regulates GABA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The NSC-induced suppression of inhibitory transmission was associated with a decrease in PPR.
source: NSC alone transiently suppressed inhibitory transmission (Figure 3D), unlike excitatory transmission (Hou et al., 2014), and this effect was associated with a decrease in PPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting Rac1 activity regulates GABA release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rac1 activity regulates GABA release.
source: NSC alone transiently suppressed inhibitory transmission (Figure 3D), unlike excitatory transmission (Hou et al., 2014), and this effect was associated with a decrease in PPR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting Rac1 activity regulates GABA release.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the NSC experiments.

claim: CK-666 bath application enhanced CB1-iLTD.
source: To directly test the role of Arp2/3 in CB1-iLTD we utilized CK-666 (100 µM), a compound that inhibits Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly by stabilizing the inactive conformation of Arp (see Figure 3G; Basu et al., 2016; Hetrick et al., 2013). CK-666 bath application enhanced CB1-iLTD (Figure 3E) suggesting that Arp2/3 participates in CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Arp2/3 participates in CB1-iLTD.
source: To directly test the role of Arp2/3 in CB1-iLTD we utilized CK-666 (100 µM), a compound that inhibits Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly by stabilizing the inactive conformation of Arp (see Figure 3G; Basu et al., 2016; Hetrick et al., 2013). CK-666 bath application enhanced CB1-iLTD (Figure 3E) suggesting that Arp2/3 participates in CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the CK-666 experiment.

claim: CK-666 had no effect on basal inhibitory transmission.
source: Unlike NSC, CK-666 had no effect on basal inhibitory transmission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), presumably because the inhibitor stabilizes the inactive (unbound) Arp2/3, but does not affect the Arp2/3 bound to actin filaments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ARPC2 protein was reduced upon CB1 activation in hippocampal neuron cultures.
source: ARPC2 protein, an essential component of the Arp2/3 complex, was reduced upon CB1 activation in hippocampal neuron cultures (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: During normal CB1-iLTD, CB1 activation-mediated Rac1 inhibition leads to removal of Arp2/3 from actin branches, and the subsequent degradation of Arp2/3.
source: We speculate that during normal CB1-iLTD, CB1 activation-mediated Rac1 inhibition leads to removal of Arp2/3 from actin branches, and the subsequent degradation of Arp2/3 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Rac1 signaling and loss of Arp2/3 likely underlie the actin remodeling required for functional and structural CB1-iLTD.
source: Together, our findings suggest that Rac1 signaling and loss of Arp2/3 likely underlie the actin remodeling required for functional and structural CB1-iLTD (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Presynaptic release machinery and cytomatrix proteins were consistently downregulated following CB1 activation.
source: Congruent with this idea, presynaptic release machinery and cytomatrix proteins were consistently downregulated (Figure 4A), whereas proteins involved in the ubiquitin/proteasome system (UPS) were upregulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Proteins involved in the ubiquitin/proteasome system (UPS) were upregulated following CB1 activation.
source: Congruent with this idea, presynaptic release machinery and cytomatrix proteins were consistently downregulated (Figure 4A), whereas proteins involved in the ubiquitin/proteasome system (UPS) were upregulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Presynaptic proteins Munc18-1, Synapsin-1, and α-Synuclein were significantly reduced by WIN (25 min, 5 µM) in hippocampal cultures.
source: We confirmed that presynaptic proteins identified in the SILAC screen, Munc18-1, Synapsin-1, and α-Synuclein, were significantly reduced by WIN (25 min, 5 µM) in hippocampal cultures (Figure 4C), suggesting rapid protein degradation upon CB1 activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CB1 activation with WIN reduced Synapsin-1 puncta intensity in CB1+ boutons despite blockade of axonal transport.
source: We found that CB1 activation with WIN reduced Synapsin-1 puncta intensity in CB1+ boutons despite blockade of axonal transport (Figure 4D), as measured by immunostaining and quantitative Airyscan microscopy, consistent with local downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CB1 activation elicits rapid downregulation of presynaptic proteins in culture and in acute slices.
source: These results suggest that CB1 activation elicits rapid downregulation of presynaptic proteins in culture and in acute slices which likely contributes to the reduction in GABA release associated with CB1-iLTD and may be mediated by degradation by the UPS.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Both net flux and the rate of degradation of K48-linked ubiquitinated proteins were significantly increased following CB1 activation.
source: We found that both net flux, that is the amount of ubiquitinated proteins degraded by the proteasome (difference between UbK48 level when proteasomal degradation is blocked and UbK48 level under normal conditions), and the rate of degradation, (measured by the ratio of UbK48 levels between blocked and basal conditions), were significantly increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CB1-iLTD was unaffected by application of the proteasomal inhibitor MG-132 (5 µM) during the baseline and induction.
source: However, to our surprise, CB1-iLTD was unaffected by application of the proteasomal inhibitor MG-132 (5 µM) during the baseline and induction (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MG-132 alone had no lasting effect on basal transmission.
source: MG-132 alone had no lasting effect on basal transmission either (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MG-132 application resulted in accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins.
source: As a positive control, MG-132 application in interleaved slices resulted in accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: While UPS activity is increased downstream of CB1 activation, proteasomal degradation is not necessary for CB1-iLTD.
source: Therefore, while UPS activity is increased downstream of CB1 activation, proteasomal degradation is not necessary for CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the MG-132 experiments.

claim: Most ubiquitination sites (~60%) on proteins decreased by CB1 activation were located in protein-protein or protein-membrane interaction domains.
source: We analyzed ubiquitination sites on a subset of proteins that were decreased by CB1 activation and found that most ubiquitination sites (~60%) were located in protein-protein or protein-membrane interaction domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; Akimov et al., 2018), indicating that ubiquitination of these proteins could impact their function.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Bath application of ziram or PYR-41 blocked CB1-iLTD.
source: Using two structurally and mechanistically distinct E1 Ubiquitin ligase inhibitors, ziram and PYR-41 (Rinetti and Schweizer, 2010), we directly tested whether ubiquitination was required for CB1-iLTD and found that bath application of ziram or PYR-41 blocked CB1-iLTD (Figure 5C) but had no significant effect on basal transmission (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ziram and PYR-41 had no significant effect on basal transmission.
source: Using two structurally and mechanistically distinct E1 Ubiquitin ligase inhibitors, ziram and PYR-41 (Rinetti and Schweizer, 2010), we directly tested whether ubiquitination was required for CB1-iLTD and found that bath application of ziram or PYR-41 blocked CB1-iLTD (Figure 5C) but had no significant effect on basal transmission (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Inhibition of ubiquitination blocked the CB1-mediated decrease in CB1+ bouton volume.
source: Moreover, inhibition of ubiquitination also blocked the CB1-mediated decrease in CB1+ bouton volume (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CB1-iLTD leads to increases in UPS proteins and is associated with functional increases in proteasomal activity.
source: In summary, CB1-iLTD leads to increases in UPS proteins and is associated with functional increases in proteasomal activity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Ubiquitination is required for protein synthesis-dependent structural and functional changes of CB1+ boutons.
source: Ubiquitination is required for protein synthesis-dependent structural and functional changes of CB1+ boutons.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: CB1-iLTD is associated with decreases in presynaptic and cytomatrix proteins, including ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1.
source: CB1-iLTD is associated with decreases in presynaptic and cytomatrix proteins, including ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1, and relies on actin dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: CB1-iLTD relies on actin dynamics.
source: CB1-iLTD is associated with decreases in presynaptic and cytomatrix proteins, including ARPC2 and WASF1/WAVE1, and relies on actin dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: While proteasomal activity increases by CB1 activation, only protein ubiquitination is required for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
source: However, while proteasomal activity increases by CB1 activation, only protein ubiquitination is required for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: CB1-iLTD involves structural changes of the presynaptic bouton that require protein synthesis.
source: We discovered that CB1-iLTD involves structural changes of the presynaptic bouton that require protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: CB1-iLTD involved actin remodeling, Rac1 and Arp2/3 signaling.
source: CB1-iLTD involved actin remodeling, Rac1 and Arp2/3 signaling.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Protein ubiquitination, but not proteasomal degradation, is responsible for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that protein ubiquitination, but not proteasomal degradation, is responsible for structural and functional CB1-iLTD.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Inhibitory presynapses can control their strength in response to CB1 activation via rapid proteostatic regulation of presynaptic structural change.
source: Together, these findings point to a mechanism by which inhibitory presynapses can control their strength in response to CB1 activation via rapid proteostatic regulation of presynaptic structural change.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary claim based on all the experimental data.

claim: Structural changes are part and parcel of postsynaptic forms of plasticity.
source: While structural changes are part and parcel of postsynaptic forms of plasticity (Bramham, 2008; Nakahata and Yasuda, 2018), and changes associated with plasticity are thought to be coordinated across the synaptic cleft, the involvement of structural changes of the presynaptic terminal in forms of long-term presynaptic plasticity are less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The involvement of structural changes of the presynaptic terminal in forms of long-term presynaptic plasticity are less clear.
source: While structural changes are part and parcel of postsynaptic forms of plasticity (Bramham, 2008; Nakahata and Yasuda, 2018), and changes associated with plasticity are thought to be coordinated across the synaptic cleft, the involvement of structural changes of the presynaptic terminal in forms of long-term presynaptic plasticity are less clear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Transient activation of CB1 receptors leads to a long-term reduction of the presynaptic CB1+ compartment volume in somatic synapses onto CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Our data show that transient activation of CB1 receptors leads to a long-term reduction of the presynaptic CB1+ compartment volume in somatic synapses onto CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data.

claim: CB1 receptors regulate actin dynamics in growth cones by directly interacting with Rac1.
source: Our findings (Figure 3) are consistent with a previous study showing that CB1 receptors regulate actin dynamics in growth cones by directly interacting with Rac1 (Njoo et al., 2015), a Rho GTPase (Mattheus et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By directly binding CB1, Rac1 can localize the WRC at the plasma membrane.
source: By directly binding CB1, Rac1 can localize the WRC which consists of WASF1/WAVE1, Cyfip1, Nap1, Abi and HSP300, at the plasma membrane (Chen et al., 2010; Eden et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The WRC is intrinsically inactive at rest.
source: The WRC is intrinsically inactive at rest (Derivery et al., 2009), but upon recruitment to the membrane by Rac1 the cytoplasmic side is opened for binding to Arp2/3 and actin (Chen et al., 2010; Eden et al., 2002), leading to dissociation of WASF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon recruitment to the membrane by Rac1 the cytoplasmic side of WRC is opened for binding to Arp2/3 and actin, leading to dissociation of WASF1.
source: The WRC is intrinsically inactive at rest (Derivery et al., 2009), but upon recruitment to the membrane by Rac1 the cytoplasmic side is opened for binding to Arp2/3 and actin (Chen et al., 2010; Eden et al., 2002), leading to dissociation of WASF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The non-neuronal, structurally homologous isoform WAVE2 was demonstrated to undergo activation-dependent dissociation from the WRC ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: Although the exact mechanism of degradation has not been shown for Arp2/3 or WASF1/WAVE1, the non-neuronal, structurally homologous isoform WAVE2 was demonstrated to undergo activation-dependent dissociation from the WRC ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Joseph et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Rac1 could be required for the degradation of WASF1/WAVE1.
source: Therefore, Rac1 could be required for the degradation of WASF1/WAVE1, but its direct involvement in presynaptic degradation of Arp2/3 is not as clear.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Rac1's direct involvement in presynaptic degradation of Arp2/3 is not as clear.
source: Therefore, Rac1 could be required for the degradation of WASF1/WAVE1, but its direct involvement in presynaptic degradation of Arp2/3 is not as clear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: Atypical coupling of CB1 to G12/13 proteins reportedly engages Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) signaling to the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: Other studies have suggested alternative signaling pathways by which structural changes occur downstream of CB1 activation. For instance, atypical coupling of CB1 to G12/13 proteins reportedly engages Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) signaling to the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Roland et al., 2014), whereas in another example, β-integrin signaling to ROCK has been implicated in a cannabinoid-mediated form of LTP (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: β-integrin signaling to ROCK has been implicated in a cannabinoid-mediated form of LTP.
source: Other studies have suggested alternative signaling pathways by which structural changes occur downstream of CB1 activation. For instance, atypical coupling of CB1 to G12/13 proteins reportedly engages Rho-associated kinase (ROCK) signaling to the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Roland et al., 2014), whereas in another example, β-integrin signaling to ROCK has been implicated in a cannabinoid-mediated form of LTP (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The signaling pathways and structural changes involved downstream of CB1 receptors seem to be synapse and cell-type-dependent.
source: Therefore, the signaling pathways and structural changes involved downstream of CB1 receptors seem to be synapse and cell-type-dependent (Steindel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Whether CB-LTD at other synapses shares similar mechanisms remains unclear.
source: Whether CB-LTD at other synapses shares similar mechanisms remains unclear.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: CB1 immunolabeling accurately approximates bouton volume.
source: CB1 bouton size was measured by immunolabeling the CB1 receptor, which, due to the extremely high density and of CB1 receptors expressed on presynaptic boutons in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, has been shown to be a reliable approximation of bouton volume (Dudok et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies in cultured neurons suggest CB1 internalization occurs.
source: Although studies in cultured neurons suggest CB1 internalization occurs (Coutts et al., 2001; Hsieh et al., 1999; Jin et al., 1999; Tappe-Theodor et al., 2007), little is known about the internalization of CB1 receptor in the intact brain, which may require longer timescales than the brief CB1 activation (25 min) we have used here (Dudok et al., 2015; Thibault et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little is known about the internalization of CB1 receptor in the intact brain.
source: Although studies in cultured neurons suggest CB1 internalization occurs (Coutts et al., 2001; Hsieh et al., 1999; Jin et al., 1999; Tappe-Theodor et al., 2007), little is known about the internalization of CB1 receptor in the intact brain, which may require longer timescales than the brief CB1 activation (25 min) we have used here (Dudok et al., 2015; Thibault et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: CB1 internalization is not protein synthesis-dependent.
source: Moreover, the CB1-mediated presynaptic shrinkage is blocked by protein synthesis inhibition whereas internalization is not protein synthesis-dependent (Hsieh et al., 1999) and is also detectable at the sub-presynaptic compartment level with Bassoon and VGAT labeling (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), two well-established markers of presynaptic structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: VGAT size showed a marked reduction in CB1+ boutons, which could reflect synaptic vesicle redistribution.
source: Intriguingly, VGAT size showed a marked reduction in CB1+ boutons, which could reflect synaptic vesicle redistribution, consistent with previous reports showing short-term CB1 activation-induced vesicle redistribution and changes in numbers of docked/primed vesicles (García-Morales et al., 2015; Ramírez-Franco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the data and previous literature.

claim: Associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from altered Ca2+ channel coupling distance with the active zone.
source: While the exact functional implications of presynaptic bouton and active zone shrinkage are yet unclear, associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from altered Ca2+ channel coupling distance with the active zone (Nakamura et al., 2015), less area for vesicular release, shift from multi- to univesicular release mode (Aubrey et al., 2017), or reorganization of transsynaptic nanocolumns (Chen et al., 2018; Glebov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from less area for vesicular release.
source: While the exact functional implications of presynaptic bouton and active zone shrinkage are yet unclear, associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from altered Ca2+ channel coupling distance with the active zone (Nakamura et al., 2015), less area for vesicular release, shift from multi- to univesicular release mode (Aubrey et al., 2017), or reorganization of transsynaptic nanocolumns (Chen et al., 2018; Glebov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim.

claim: Associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from shift from multi- to univesicular release mode.
source: While the exact functional implications of presynaptic bouton and active zone shrinkage are yet unclear, associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from altered Ca2+ channel coupling distance with the active zone (Nakamura et al., 2015), less area for vesicular release, shift from multi- to univesicular release mode (Aubrey et al., 2017), or reorganization of transsynaptic nanocolumns (Chen et al., 2018; Glebov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from reorganization of transsynaptic nanocolumns.
source: While the exact functional implications of presynaptic bouton and active zone shrinkage are yet unclear, associated changes in neurotransmitter release may result from altered Ca2+ channel coupling distance with the active zone (Nakamura et al., 2015), less area for vesicular release, shift from multi- to univesicular release mode (Aubrey et al., 2017), or reorganization of transsynaptic nanocolumns (Chen et al., 2018; Glebov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CB1 activation significantly upregulated proteins involved in protein synthesis and processing pathways.
source: We found that CB1 activation significantly upregulated proteins involved in protein synthesis and processing pathways (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The increase in initiation factors and ribosomal proteins suggests that plasticity likely triggers an enhanced translational capacity.
source: This increase in initiation factors and ribosomal proteins suggests that plasticity likely triggers an enhanced translational capacity which is consistent with our previous findings using Fluorescent Noncanonical Amino acid Tagging (FUNCAT) (Younts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the SILAC data and previous findings.

claim: mRNAs for Arp2/3, WAVE1, and β-actin have been detected in axonal preparations.
source: mRNAs for Arp2/3, WAVE1, and β-actin have been detected in axonal preparations and their synthesis may be important for axon formation (Donnelly et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synthesis of Arp2/3, WAVE1, and β-actin may be important for axon formation.
source: mRNAs for Arp2/3, WAVE1, and β-actin have been detected in axonal preparations and their synthesis may be important for axon formation (Donnelly et al., 2013; Spillane et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In CB1-iLTD, protein synthesis seems to mediate the change in presynaptic structure via the UPS, rather than direct synthesis of actin regulators.
source: However, in CB1-iLTD, protein synthesis seems to mediate the change in presynaptic structure via the UPS, rather than direct synthesis of actin regulators.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Upregulation of UPS components represents an activity-dependent synthesis of regulatory elements in the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation pathway.
source: Our finding of downregulation of many presynaptic proteins and upregulation of components of the UPS suggested to us that perhaps this upregulation represents an activity-dependent synthesis of regulatory elements in the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the SILAC data.

claim: It is likely that additional 'plasticity-related' proteins are synthesized or degraded in the hours that follow iLTD induction.
source: It is likely that additional 'plasticity-related' proteins are synthesized or degraded in the hours that follow iLTD induction.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the timing of measurements.

claim: Activity-dependent local presynaptic synthesis of UPS machinery has never been demonstrated.
source: While activity-dependent local presynaptic synthesis of UPS machinery has never been demonstrated, there is strong evidence that presynaptic function can be regulated by expression of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases and degradation of select presynaptic proteins.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: There is strong evidence that presynaptic function can be regulated by expression of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases and degradation of select presynaptic proteins.
source: While activity-dependent local presynaptic synthesis of UPS machinery has never been demonstrated, there is strong evidence that presynaptic function can be regulated by expression of specific E3 ubiquitin ligases and degradation of select presynaptic proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the discussion that follows and citations.

claim: SCRAPPER an E3 ligase has been shown to target presynaptic proteins like RIM1, synaptophysin, and Munc18.
source: For example, SCRAPPER an E3 ligase has been shown to target presynaptic proteins like RIM1, synaptophysin, and Munc18 (Yao et al., 2007), amongst other proteins with high similarity to those identified in our SILAC dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SCRAPPER KO has been shown to impair neurotransmitter release, short-term plasticity and presynaptic LTP.
source: Moreover, SCRAPPER KO has been shown to impair neurotransmitter release, short-term plasticity and presynaptic LTP (Koga et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The tight coupling of translation and degradation in the context of synaptic plasticity was described previously.
source: The tight coupling of translation and degradation in the context of synaptic plasticity was described previously (Klein et al., 2015) and is presumed to occur widely in the brain as a means of maintaining proteostasis over the course of plastic changes (Biever et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2008; Hanus and Schuman, 2013; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rapid activity-dependent degradation could be mediated by the recently discovered neuron-specific proteasome complex (NMP).
source: This rapid activity-dependent degradation could be mediated by the recently discovered neuron-specific proteasome complex (NMP) (Ramachandran et al., 2018), although this complex is believed to target non-ubiquitinated substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Protein degradation has been shown to regulate presynaptic silencing, specifically by degradation of presynaptic proteins such as RIM1 and Munc13.
source: Protein degradation has also been shown to regulate presynaptic silencing, specifically by degradation of presynaptic proteins such as RIM1 and Munc13 (Jiang et al., 2010) and CB1-mediated suppression of transmission at excitatory synapses via degradation of Munc18 (Schmitz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CB1-mediated suppression of transmission at excitatory synapses occurs via degradation of Munc18.
source: Protein degradation has also been shown to regulate presynaptic silencing, specifically by degradation of presynaptic proteins such as RIM1 and Munc13 (Jiang et al., 2010) and CB1-mediated suppression of transmission at excitatory synapses via degradation of Munc18 (Schmitz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity in response to neuron silencing has been associated with degradation of select presynaptic proteins.
source: Homeostatic plasticity in response to neuron silencing has also been associated with degradation of select presynaptic proteins (Lazarevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Protein degradation by the UPS is not directly required for CB1-iLTD.
source: However, our data strongly support the idea that protein degradation by the UPS is not directly required for CB1-iLTD, but likely does occur quickly after CB1 activation, as indicated by rapid loss of presynaptic proteins measured with both SILAC and western blot (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data.

claim: Rapid reduction in protein levels presumably occurs as a consequence of enhanced UPS activity.
source: This rapid reduction in protein levels presumably occurs as a consequence of enhanced UPS activity (Figure 5), but we cannot exclude that a different mechanism could be involved including reduced synthesis (Dörrbaum et al., 2020) or other protein degradation pathways, such as autophagy (Liang and Sigrist, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim with acknowledgment of alternative possibilities.

claim: Ubiquitination is required for CB1-iLTD, likely by controlling the trafficking, interactions, or the activity of its substrates, upstream of degradation.
source: We demonstrated that ubiquitination is required for CB1-iLTD, likely by controlling the trafficking, interactions, or the activity of its substrates, upstream of degradation (Hamilton and Zito, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data and citation to previous literature.

claim: A previous study showed that inhibition of protein ubiquitination and degradation increased miniature EPSCs/IPSCs in cultured neurons.
source: A previous study showed that inhibition of protein ubiquitination and degradation increased miniature EPSCs/IPSCs in cultured neurons, suggesting an important role for these processes in maintaining normal neurotransmitter release (Rinetti and Schweizer, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: This study is the first to describe a mechanism of long-term presynaptic structural and functional plasticity that relies on ubiquitination.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first to describe a mechanism of long-term presynaptic structural and functional plasticity that relies on ubiquitination.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The regulation of presynaptic ubiquitination is likely achieved through the targeted expression of different E2 and E3 ubiquitin ligases.
source: The regulation of presynaptic ubiquitination is likely achieved through the targeted expression of different E2 and E3 ubiquitin ligases (Hallengren et al., 2013; Koga et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2007) or via presynaptic cytomatrix proteins themselves (Chen et al., 2003; Ivanova et al., 2016; Waites et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Presynaptic structural dynamics and UPS activity are tightly linked.
source: This raises the possibility that presynaptic structural dynamics and UPS activity are tightly linked.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings.

claim: CB1 activation via eCBs, as well as exogenous cannabinoids like Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), can influence cognition, goal-directed behaviors, sensory processing and other critical brain functions.
source: CB1 activation via eCBs, as well as exogenous cannabinoids like Δ9- tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive ingredient in marijuana, can influence cognition, goal-directed behaviors, sensory processing and other critical brain functions (Araque et al., 2017; Augustin and Lovinger, 2018; Häring et al., 2012; Heifets and Castillo, 2009; Hoffman and Lupica, 2013; Zlebnik and Cheer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cannabinoid signaling has been implicated in several brain disorders.
source: Cannabinoid signaling has also been implicated in several brain disorders (Zou and Kumar, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Autism is broadly associated with changes in synaptic protein levels.
source: Autism is broadly associated with changes in synaptic protein levels, but also disruption of CB1-LTD (Busquets-Garcia et al., 2014; Chakrabarti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Autism is associated with disruption of CB1-LTD.
source: Autism is broadly associated with changes in synaptic protein levels, but also disruption of CB1-LTD (Busquets-Garcia et al., 2014; Chakrabarti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In a mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), eCB-mediated plasticity in the hippocampus, striatum, prefrontal cortex is impaired.
source: In particular, in a mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome (FXS), the most common monogenic cause of autism, where RNA-binding protein, Fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) is deleted (Bagni and Zukin, 2019), eCB-mediated plasticity in the hippocampus, striatum, prefrontal cortex is impaired (Jung et al., 2012; Maccarrone et al., 2010; Martin et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018b; Zhang and Alger, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Changes in the eCB mobilization in FXS may explain some of the impairment in eCB-mediated plasticity.
source: Although changes in the eCB mobilization in FXS may explain some of the impairment (Jung et al., 2012; Maccarrone et al., 2010; Zhang and Alger, 2010), the role of FMRP in the regulation of local presynaptic protein synthesis may also play a role (but see Jung et al., 2012), although this remains to be tested (Busquets-Garcia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by imbalanced proteostasis, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), resulting in pathological accumulations of misfolded proteins.
source: Many neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by imbalanced proteostasis, including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), resulting in pathological accumulations of misfolded proteins (Klaips et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: WIN treatment in animal models of AD and PD has been shown to be neuroprotective and to alleviate cognitive and motor symptoms.
source: WIN treatment in animal models of AD and PD has been shown to be neuroprotective and to alleviate cognitive and motor symptoms (Basavarajappa et al., 2017), potentially through the ability of the CB1 receptor to regulate synaptic proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: WIN treatment may be neuroprotective through the ability of the CB1 receptor to regulate synaptic proteostasis.
source: WIN treatment in animal models of AD and PD has been shown to be neuroprotective and to alleviate cognitive and motor symptoms (Basavarajappa et al., 2017), potentially through the ability of the CB1 receptor to regulate synaptic proteostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the findings and previous literature.
